query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature plastic strain and toughness of fusion plasma‐facing structural alloys are governed by the state of grain boundary chemistry, such that targeted dopant additions that promote beneficial segregation at grain boundaries enhance both grain boundary cohesion and the modulation of dislocation/grain-boundary interactions.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline structural alloy for fusion plasma-facing components with conventional grain boundary chemistry and a controlled, reproducible microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled alloying dopants that selectively segregate to grain boundaries without causing bulk phase changes.
generation.conditions: In situ mechanical testing under fusion-relevant high-temperature conditions (800–1200°C) with controlled loading in a simulated plasma environment, ensuring similar grain sizes and processing history for all samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified grain boundary composition featuring dopant segregation that strengthens the intergranular bonds and alters dislocation nucleation and motion at the boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Dopant-induced segregation enhances grain boundary cohesion by reducing the propensity for grain boundary sliding and intergranular cavitation, and simultaneously alters the interaction of dislocations with these boundaries, leading to improved strain hardening and delayed crack initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped baseline, the doped alloy will exhibit increased toughness and sustained or enhanced plastic strain at high temperatures, indicated by higher yield strengths, extended ductility, and reduced intergranular cracking during in situ high-temperature tests.
generation.baseline: Identical alloy processed under the same conditions but without the targeted dopant additions (i.e., with unmodified grain boundary chemistry).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in alloys with comparable grain sizes and microstructures, and under high-temperature conditions (800–1200°C); effects may differ if the temperature is significantly below or above this range, or if dopant levels induce secondary phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in toughness and plastic strain is uncertain and may depend on the specific dopant chemistry and its solubility. Additionally, the influence of high-temperature oxidation could complicate the observed effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same alloy system: one set with the engineered dopant additions designed to modify the grain boundary chemistry, and a control set without the dopants. Subject both sets to in situ high-temperature mechanical testing (800–1200°C) under identical loading and environmental conditions in a simulated fusion plasma environment. Post-test, perform advanced microscopy (TEM/APT) to analyze grain boundary chemistry and dislocation behavior.
measurements: High-temperature tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness)
Grain boundary composition and segregation profiles via atom probe tomography (APT)
Dislocation structures and grain boundary sliding observations via transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped samples do not show statistically significant improvements in toughness and plastic strain (or display no measurable changes in grain boundary chemistry and associated dislocation interactions) compared to the control set, then the hypothesis that dopant-induced grain boundary chemistry governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness will be falsified.

How the grain boundary affects the deformation behaviour and thus improves the mechanical properties of HEAs becomes a primary question for researchers. In previous work, Yu et al. observed that a CrFeCoNiPd alloy had higher continuous steady strain hardening than that in other single-phase HEAs with similar grain sizes at ambient temperature. They also hypothesized that plastic deformation at room temperature was primarily involved in the 1/2 <110> {111} full dislocation. Lu et al. simulated the deposition and annealing process of AlCoCrCuFeNi HEAs and observed that a phase of the cluster structure was transformed from BCC to FCC. The clustering in HEAs has a significant effect on the phase transition. Huang et al. simulated the glass transition temperature of Al–Cu–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs using molecular dynamics (MD). Li et al. simulated the structural transformation process of a AlCrCoCuFeNi HEA at different cooling rates by molecular dynamics. Few studies have focused on the influence of the grain boundary on the strength of high entropy alloys. occupying_moves.lever: alloying to modify grain boundary chemistry
occupying_moves.technique: in situ high-temperature mechanical testing combined with advanced microscopy (e.g., TEM/APT)

chosen.lever: alloying to modify grain boundary chemistry
chosen.technique: in situ high-temperature mechanical testing combined with advanced electron microscopy (TEM/atom probe)
chosen.conditions: Comparative experiments on baseline versus doped structural alloys conducted over 800–1200°C under controlled loading in a simulated fusion environment, ensuring that only the grain boundary chemistry is varied
chosen.why: This move directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are governed by the state of grain boundary chemistry—specifically, that controlled dopant additions lead to beneficial segregation effects which modify dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding. By comparing doped and undoped samples under identical high-temperature conditions using well‐established experimental techniques, the study isolates the effect of composition on the microstructural evolution and mechanical response, thereby addressing the open question with a standard, reproducible approach in materials science.
